front: Which command enables IPv6 forwarding on a basic IOS router?
back: Global `ipv6 unicast-routing`. Addressed interfaces alone can answer local traffic without providing inter-interface forwarding.

front: Why does a link-local next hop need scope?
back: The same address can exist on different links. Its useful neighbor identity includes the local exit interface.

front: Required IPv6 static-route form for a link-local next hop?
back: `ipv6 route destination/prefix-length exit-interface link-local-next-hop`. Substitute the actual prefix, interface and neighbor values.

front: IPv6 default-route prefix?
back: ::/0. It matches all IPv6 addresses but is used only when no longer installed prefix matches.

front: IPv6 host-route prefix length?
back: /128. All address bits are specified, so the route matches one destination.

front: Ordinary static route distance, and unusable distance?
back: Default static distance 1; distance 255 is not usable for installation.

front: How does an IPv6 floating static become selected?
back: It has higher distance than the preferred candidate to the same prefix. It can install after primary withdrawal if the backup path remains usable.

front: Read [5/0] in an IPv6 static route.
back: Administrative distance 5, metric 0. The values do not mean five hops and zero packet loss.

front: What does fully specified mean for an IPv6 static route?
back: Both exit interface and next hop are supplied. Ethernet still needs Neighbor Discovery to resolve the next hop's MAC.

front: Problem with an Ethernet interface-only route to a remote IPv6 LAN?
back: It treats remote destinations as on-link and can attempt ND for them on the transit segment. Name the adjacent router rather than relying on unconfigured proxy behavior.

front: What does a non-link-local next-hop-only route need?
back: A usable resolving route to that next hop without self-dependency. A connected transit prefix provides this in the lab; do not assume default-based recursion is enabled.

front: What do C, L and S mean in the IPv6 route table?
back: C: connected prefix. L: local interface address, usually /128. S: static route. A remote static /128 is different from a local L /128.

front: Which command shows IPv6 neighbor bindings?
back: `show ipv6 neighbors`. Entries include interface scope; the cache is not an inventory of all peer addresses.

front: Does a stale IPv6 neighbor entry prove failure?
back: No. It lacks recent reachability confirmation. Incomplete means resolution has not completed and can be temporary; persistent failures justify further checks.

front: Why can IOS ask for Output Interface during a link-local ping?
back: The destination is meaningful only on one link. Supply the local exit interface. Prompt availability and wording can vary by simulator image.

front: How is an IPv6 route destination written?
back: As prefix/length, such as 2001:db8:20::/64. Do not append an IPv4 dotted mask.

front: Does lower distance make /64 beat an installed /128?
back: No. A matching /128 wins forwarding because it is longer. Distance selects candidates for the same prefix before forwarding compares installed entries.

front: Does an ordinary floating static detect every failure beyond its next hop?
back: No. It takes over when the preferred route becomes ineligible; a remote service failure may leave that route installed.

front: Does failed ND for an installed /128 automatically make a matching /64 the forwarding choice?
back: No. While the /128 remains installed, its longer match still selects it. Investigate its scoped next hop.

front: Why can a router-sourced ping work while a client-sourced ping fails?
back: The peer may know the router transit source but lack a return route to the client prefix. Compare actual sources and reverse lookups.
